study.title: Modulation effect of acupuncture treatment on chronic neck and shoulder pain in female patients: Evidence from periaqueductal gray-based functional connectivity
study.study_design: Prospective pre-post within-subject neuroimaging study with matched healthy control comparison group
study.blinding: Clinical pain experts assessing diagnosis were blinded to the study; acupuncturist was blinded to the study; clinical psychologist conducting neuropsychological assessments was blinded to experimental procedures
study.population: Thirty right-handed female patients with chronic neck and shoulder pain and thirty pain-free age- and sex-matched healthy controls recruited from the same geographic area
study.inclusion_criteria: (1) complaints of neck and shoulder pain (with or without radiating arm pain) for at least 6 months with cervical degeneration in X-ray and MRI; (2) no pain in other parts of body; and (3) not receiving any treatment within the last one month before this study
study.exclusion_criteria: (1) history of neck trauma; (2) vertebral body or spinal canal cancer, tuberculosis, or severe osteoporosis; (3) history of neck surgery or presence of congenital malformation of the cervical vertebrae; (4) pregnant or breastfeeding; and (5) presence of a severe systemic disease such as tumors, or digestive system disease; and (6) MRI contraindications

extraction_notes.note: No sham acupuncture or control acupuncture arm was included. This is a pre-post study with a healthy control comparison group only, not a randomized controlled trial. No randomization is reported.
No quantitative expectancy, credibility, or blinding success measures were reported. No tools such as CEQ, PEI, or allocation guessing were administered.
No adverse events section is reported in the paper. It is unclear whether adverse events were monitored or assessed.
The paper states the trial was 'retrospectively registered' on February 06, 2018 (ChiCTR2000030383), which raises potential reporting bias concerns.
Deqi was described qualitatively as a procedural requirement (soreness, numbness, distention, heaviness). No quantitative deqi instrument (e.g., MASS, SAS) was used. No deqi scores are reported.

Neuropsychological measure values for patients are described as 'mean (standard error)' in the table note but this may be standard deviation. The paper states 'Continuous variables are reported as mean (standard error)' — preserved as reported.

The p-values reported in Table 2 (e.g., 0.024, 0.008) for cluster peaks represent the FWE-corrected cluster-level p-values as described, but the exact statistic type (t, F, z) is not specified in the table.
The paper refers to 'two-sample paired t-test' throughout but the term is non-standard; it appears to mean a standard paired samples t-test within the CNSP group across timepoints.

The study reports pgCG (pregenual cingulate gyrus) coordinates as (−4, 48, 12) and sgCG (subgenual cingulate gyrus) coordinates as (−4, 48, 10) — these are nearly identical. This may reflect a table or OCR error or very similar coordinates. Extracted as reported.

The paper references Figure S1 for the seed location visualization, which is available as supplementary material not provided in this PDF. The seed coordinates are reported in the main text and are extractable.

The paper does not report whether motion exclusion criteria (e.g., framewise displacement thresholds) were applied beyond motion correction and regression. No subjects appear to have been excluded for excessive motion.
Only female patients were included. The study explicitly identifies this as a limitation, noting future studies should include both sexes.

The correlation between PAG-pIns FC percent change and PCS percent change (R = 0.637) uses percent change calculations where the denominator is the pre-acupuncture value. The sign and direction (higher FC change = greater PCS reduction) is stated in text but the axes labeling in Figure 5 shows 'percent change of PCS score' on Y axis and 'percent change of PAG-pIns FC' on X axis with a positive slope — suggesting both increase together. This is consistent with the interpretation that greater FC recovery correlates with greater catastrophizing reduction (improvement on PCS = lower score, but the percent change as computed may be positive for both).
No information is provided on acupuncture needle brand, gauge, or manufacturer.
The paper does not report whether acupuncture sessions were delivered daily without interruption across all four weeks or whether there were any breaks in treatment.
